speaker: Mr Jackson Lam
text: asked the Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (a) whether police risk-assessment tools will be recalibrated to prioritise cases involving children who are missing from contact for extended periods; (b) whether an automatic supervisory review will be triggered after defined time lapses for such cases; and (c) how technology, such as inter-agency databases or alerts, will support faster child location efforts by the police.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam
text: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming) (for the Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs): Mr Speaker, may I seek your permission to answer Question Nos 26 and 27 filed by Mr Jackson Lam and Mr Gabriel Lam on today's Order Paper?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Goh Pei Ming: My reply will also cover questions for written answer filed by Ms Valerie Lee and Ms Diana Pang for today's Sitting.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Desmond has earlier set out the Government’s views on it.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In 2020, after Megan's death was uncovered, the Police reviewed their handling of the case.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There were two rounds of police reports filed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The first report was made in January 2020 by Megan’s grandmother.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Further police reports were made in July 2020, by Megan's grandmother and father.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The IO had assessed this as a case of child discipline with low safety concerns based on the information that she was presented with at that time.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Following the report, the IO attempted to contact Megan's mother over the next two weeks, but could not reach her.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: She did not follow up beyond that because she was then deployed for COVID-19 related duties.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Despite this, the case would normally have been followed up if the IO and her supervisor had escalated the case to the regular case review sessions in the first place.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The subsequent Police reports concerning Megan were referred to the regular case review sessions, and this eventually led to the discovery of Megan's death and the arrests of the perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: For missing person reports, the Police have established procedures to guide the follow-up.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Specifically, the Police accord priority to missing vulnerable persons as they may be at higher risk, regardless of the duration they have been missing and this includes young children.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Cases of missing vulnerable persons are escalated to the regular case review sessions with supervisors for monitoring and guidance.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is standard procedure for the Police to work with other Government agencies to locate missing persons, including sharing the data of the missing persons.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Where necessary, the Police may also issue appeals for information to seek the public's assistance.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Police do not track the duration taken to close a case.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There are many factors that can affect the length of an investigation.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This includes the wide range of offences with varying complexities, as well as the need to work with different partners as part of the investigation process.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There are internal controls in place to ensure that cases are followed up promptly.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These include a daily case review process for supervisors to provide guidance on the cases, and multiple levels of supervision and regular checks throughout the investigation.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But the Police have also continued to strengthen these processes and systems.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In particular, the Police have made several enhancements.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Specialised training is provided to FVT officers to equip them with the knowledge and skillsets to handle these cases, such as how to engage the victims sensitively, as well as how to work closely and more integrated with other agencies.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In particular, when Police come across a case of suspected child abuse, or when MSF receives an urgent report on high-risk cases through their National Anti-Violence and Sexual Harassment Helpline (NAVH), the Police will work with MSF Protective Service for safety planning and social intervention for the family and child.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This may include the activation of MSF's Domestic Violence Emergency Response Team (DVERT), a round-the-clock service launched in 2023 to provide immediate help to high-risk domestic violence cases with immediate safety concerns.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: DVERT officers would respond on-site to conduct a professional assessment and make urgent arrangements for the victims to be relocated or placed in alternative care for their safety, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: DVERT officers are also empowered under the Women's Charter to issue Emergency Orders (EOs) at the scene and to provide immediate safety for the victim.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: To strengthen IOs' efficiency and supervisory capabilities, the Police have also harnessed technology for the review of cases.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: They have implemented technological solutions to trigger automatic notifications to IOs and their supervisors to complete time-sensitive tasks promptly.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Our frontline Police Officers bear a heavy responsibility to protect lives.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: They take this responsibility seriously and perform their duties with commitment and professionalism.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The demands on our Police Officers continue to increase.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: They often have to make difficult judgement calls every day in the course of their duties.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In this case, the lapse arose because two officers, who were under pressure, did not follow the established operating procedure.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It was a serious breach, and it resulted in a tragic outcome.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Police will learn from this, and reinforce procedures and training for its officers.

speaker: (Resumption for supplementary questions)
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central): Thank you, Sir.

speaker: (Resumption for supplementary questions)
text: I welcome, in particular, the groundbreaking step that all child losses, in future, will be independently reviewed.

speaker: (Resumption for supplementary questions)
text: Yet, we must also do so in a way that sensitively protects the officers directly involved in each child loss case, because they bear the emotional brunt of these cases.

speaker: (Resumption for supplementary questions)
text: And so I think the only way we can do so is if we have, first, in the child protection ecosystem, a culture of collective ownership, and this must go beyond taking collective responsibility when things go bad.

speaker: (Resumption for supplementary questions)
text: It must mean a culture of ever more equal partnership when things are not bad, so that when things do go bad, we have the capacity to first, band together, grief together, cope together and support each other first.

speaker: (Resumption for supplementary questions)
text: So, beyond system enhancements, my question is how does the Ministry plan to build up and strengthen this culture of collective ownership in our child protective ecosystem?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: With that correction behind us, Sir, I will address the Member's two questions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The sector is working together and working with the community and the public to prevent harm from occurring.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is a challenging and difficult and onerous responsibility which the sector bears and must bear, for the protection of children and vulnerable persons, whether spouses, persons with disability, the elderly, and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And when a tragic outcome happens – whether hurt, serious hurt or a death – everyone who has or might have had an opportunity or a touchpoint feels this, not just organisationally and sectorally, but individually.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And it is a question of "what ifs?" And as I said, it is prevention work, and our officers, both frontline as well as in the community, engage a lot of people all the time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So that, for us, in handling cases like these, it is a balance between, on the one hand, transparency and accountability, which is important to maintain public trust and confidence, and confidence by the parents that children will be taken care of by the community; and on the other hand, making sure that the morale, the determination and the will of our frontliners and our social workers is not broken.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Because if they are demoralised, if they feel that this work is too much to bear, then it will be even harder for us to maintain this sentinel system to protect the most vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, the Member is quite right in that when things go wrong – and in this case, things went wrong – we bear it as a sector, we bear it as agencies responsible, having interacted with, or having had opportunity to interact with the cases.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Certainly, when officers have breached protocols, as you have heard Minister of State Goh, and as I have mentioned earlier, internal reviews and action have to be taken.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But the burden is on the whole sector, as well as on the organisations concerned.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, we strike a balance between both very paramount considerations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: When I gave my response earlier, you would see graphically in your mind that child protection work involves rings of concentric circles, and they all have to work collectively together, the wider circle being members of the public, neighbours, colleagues, strangers, lending a helping hand or reporting abuse, so that the inner rings, community organisations like schools, preschools, general practitioners, clinics, can take a closer look and also report.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For an even inner ring of child protection case management agencies, including the Protective Service, to be able to intervene, offer help, protect the child through safety plans, and in the most high risk cases, intervene statutorily, with the Police, with the Courts, if necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For all that to work, we need to continue to build up this culture of collective ownership, of relationships between organisations in this safety net.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As I said in my reply at the end, we certainly have protocols, standard operating procedures, and common language and screening guides.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: All these are important so that things do not get missed, so that people can have the benefit of experienced people who have come out with these protocols for us to follow, so that our system can get better.

But that is no substitute for the importance of a strong inter-agency collaborative relationship between one another, all wanting to work together, all knowing each other and all imbibing that common vision and mission of taking care of the most vulnerable.
So, I agree with the Member that it is work that is underway and it is a continuous work in progress, as new officers join the system.
The Member asked why there was a review in 2025.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will run through the list of those who have filed questions.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Speaker, I thank the Ministers for their reply.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The initial reporting of the case in the media kind of pinned the blame on the social service agency Beyond Social Services that was involved, and a few community and social practitioners actually spoke up on social media about the optics of the reporting.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think, retrospectively, the question is then, how can we better report or communicate when such tragedies happen, in light of also encouraging collective ownership and culture?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My second question refers to conversations with preschool educators.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On one hand, one anecdote was, as much as educators want to balance building rapport with parents and they do ask when they find injuries on the children and they need to ask in a polite and non-offensive way to just clarify how injuries that might have occurred when they bring their child to the centre.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, the question is: how does the Ministry help to support preschools in balancing this rapport with parents that preschool educators have to constantly balance?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another question by preschool educators was when a child with non-verbal or with special needs might present with injuries that parents may attribute to falls, that it is only the parents' account that is taken into consideration.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What advice would we give to preschools to assess in those cases, how much of parents' accounts to believe and whether or not to make a report with NAVH, nevertheless?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A last question from preschool educators is, after the abused child returns to a centre, they may also exhibit some of this abusive or violent or inappropriate behaviour to their peers as well.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can teachers be better prepared for these scenarios?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My last supplementary question references an initiative by MSF and Koufu that was launched in August this year, where 77 food court managers were trained by MSF to be the eyes and ears of the community and highlight NAVH hotline and the work that they do.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, my question is, how do we expand such initiatives, like Minister Desmond Lee mentioned, the rings of concentric circles where a society's collective responsibility to protect the vulnerable?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The balance, as I said earlier, is between setting out the facts as to what happened and on the other hand, keeping the sector cohesive as a whole.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The aim is to reflect on what happened and see how those gaps should be closed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so, there was not and should not be an intention to point fingers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the same time, the public expect some accountability and laying out of the facts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That is what happened in the report of the independent Panel.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It was not the intention, but if that was perceived, we have apologised as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For preschools, because they deal with very young children from infants to the age of six, sometimes, it is very hard to discern what is actually happening.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And that is why we need two things.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the one hand, with experience, we produce protocols, guides to empower our frontliners, including preschool leaders and preschool teachers and carers, to be able to identify concerns and possible child abuse.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, as I said earlier, if they detect something of concern, they can report.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It will be for the social workers to offer more targeted support and for the protection agencies to intervene and make safe for the child.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Having said that, I understand that there is a relationship between the preschool and the preschool teachers, and the parents and children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we would like to encourage them, step forward if they want to play a part, and we will work with them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Notwithstanding that, we have extended the Question Time today, I request all Members and Ministers to keep your replies succinct.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome Minister's announcement of the new social service coordination centre by MSF and the usage of analytic tools to help with the detection and reporting.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I do believe that any risk factor, while it can be a predisposition, it could not be a predetermination of outcome.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But let me set out the context first.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I asked about reforms which include independent oversight bodies, because when there are clear independence and separation between report monitoring and service delivery, that could be an uplifting of standards, quality and trust.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, my first question arises from other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In New Zealand, there is an independent children's monitor that looks into compliance and of child protection laws, and it is an independent crown entity that reports to the public.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the United Kingdom (UK), there is also the Office for Standards in Education, Children's Services and Skills, or Ofsted.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ofsted does not just look into early childhood education but the whole gamut of the child's growing up years as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And whether it is a comparative study of overseas jurisdictions or engaging our sector to better strengthen our system, which we have been doing and will continue to do, all that will be taken on board, and I thank the Member for his suggestions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Likewise, for audit, I have talked about practice audits, I have talked about various ways in which we ensure some consistency across the whole sector – because there are many organisations and many individuals involved in protection work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I said earlier, there are screening guides, there are reporting guides, there are protocols in place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All these are important ways, on top of practice audits, to maintain and uphold standards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And I take the Member's suggestions on board.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Following the Review Panel's findings, practitioners, such as the social workers, were very quick to point out that that there needed to be greater support for professionals in the child protection space, rather than simply having more standard operating procedures, guidelines, protocols, as what Minister has said.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: So, I would like to ask what are the plans to upskill practitioners in child protection and how can we elevate the persistent workload concerns in the sector?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My second question is: how does the Ministry intend to address the Review Panel's findings that there appeared to be some fear of reporting to the authorities?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must surely do all we can to encourage cases to be reported and to inculcate a no-fault culture, even if suspicions of child abuse later turn out to be inaccurate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Review Panel flagged inter-agency coordination failures as one of its findings.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There seems to be no clear system for sharing updates among Child Protective Service, ECDA, Beyond Social Services, the preschool and even the Police.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And because of that, agencies appeared to have treated concerns as somebody else's responsibility and therefore, resulting in some form of inertia.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Therefore, Panel recommended establishing a centralised case management platform for high-risk child cases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I had mentioned in my reply that the system can work only if our frontliners have the skills, the judgement, the experience and the morale to keep this sentinel safety net strong and therefore, that is a priority.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Therefore, capability building and strengthening resourcing was point number one in my response.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I would not repeat what I said earlier, bearing in mind Speaker's admonition about long replies.
Fear of reporting, I have also addressed that in my reply.

In the Break the Silence campaign, we aim to encourage members of the public, if you hear something, see something that is not right, if you hear children screaming, if you hear shouting, beating, if you know your neighbour, ask if they need help, if they need some support, and if you are concerned, report.
For frontline agencies like preschools, schools, there is outreach, there is engagement for preschools every year, for leaders, Protective Service will go out and do a refresher.
There are protocols in place, there are timelines for reporting.
All these are in place, but ultimately it is about their sense of collective responsibility and mission, which I also mentioned earlier.
Sharing of updates, the Panel had a very good recommendation as to make sure that when things go wrong, you do not just do a bilateral with the organisation, you do not just do an internal review.
Share it more widely with the sector so that we all can strengthen our processes and benefit.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I just have two supplementary questions: one on a recommended response and the second on reporting.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On response, can we consider the review requiring a protocol where physical verification of a child who is a subject of a report, either missing or suspected child abuse, is actually closed within a certain timeline before the case is closed or escalated to the next level?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can we consider a mandatory child safety reporting framework so as to go beyond guidelines?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And to refine it with a tier one where it imposes a legal obligation on professionals and frontliners, say teachers, doctors, childcare operators, to report any such cases.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a high bar but it helps us close the gap.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the second tier, we could cover community leaders, volunteers, neighbours even, and protect them with a good faith protection clause, so as to remove any fear of reporting or repercussions.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These two aspects on response and reporting could help us close the gap on this very important issue.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is physical, in-person sighting for children of concern, children at risk.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For legal reporting, I think I have answered that earlier in my response.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are legal thresholds that mandate reporting, both for certain institutions as well as for public.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But having said that, the Member is talking about raising concerns even at lower thresholds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When a child comes to school or to childcare centre or goes to a community organisation with bruises, it is a very young child, the first thing you would ask the caregiver and parents is, what happened?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Quite often, the response is "fell down", "child discipline".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And for most people, well, okay, we take the parents' word for it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Then, over time, if there are certain dots that when you connect them, then you realise that actually this is a bit more concerning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Is there some trigger that might be more sinister than discipline or an accident?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And it has got to do with judgement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Yes, we have protocols in place and these – I will not say tick boxes because it does give a wrong impression – but they indeed are based on past cases and experience, and they guide frontliners in deciding what to ask, when to ask, when to raise concerns, and who to raise concerns to.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, the Member mentioned high bar of reporting, but we are talking about raising concerns with the family, with social workers and with NAVH so that we can act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We want to make sure that all of these are in place and people understand that they can do so and seek help and report, so that we can take a look.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It pains me as a mom to hear what has happened and it continues to pain me every day.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I hope this will be first and the last time I hear this, and this will never happen again.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: With so many agencies and parties involved, too many ingredients may spoil the soup.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: So, who is ultimately in charge of this, and what they can do when this happens again?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think the Member is right in that when there is an abuse case or suspected abuse case, often one of the contributing reasons could be caregiver burdens and stress, though there could be other triggers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Particularly when: (a) a safety plan has to be established and (b) removal must take place, one or the other.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, that is how it is carried out on the ground, and a lot of judgement and empathy is involved.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Having said that, the centrality of child safety is foundational.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I have always been very inspired by how our Municipal Services Office has been improving our neighbourhoods, and I am heartened to know that a similar concept, a social services coordination centre will help to improve the lives of our people.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Has the Government any programmes in place aimed at preventing child abuse in the first place, going upstream, with a particular focus on providing support and resources to parents who might face challenges coping with their child's behaviour?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This can include targeted counselling services or producing resource guides issued to parents and tailored to the age of their children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I said, the foundational principle is that parents are responsible for children and by far and away, parents do their best for the children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But when they face stressors or when they are grappling with issues, we need to provide help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, upstream work, preventive work is key, not just early risk families, but also parents at large.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have a whole range of programmes, both in institutions, like in schools and preschools, in programmes like KidSTART and others, Triple P, and many others that seek to empower or provide useful information to parents in their caregiving of their children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, that is available and will continue to work with partners to strengthen this.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that MSF has plans to train up the frontline officers.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But before we get there, will MSF consider getting an independent auditor to review the hotline records, so that the case registration failures are not only flagged up internally, but also externally verified.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And as I said earlier in my main response, it is not just within the child protection management agencies who are looking at the cases, they are progressively and expeditiously reaching out to community organisations and social service agencies that are not within the core child protection case management agency group to ask them to surface cases, and have another look.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I wish to first declare that I am a family law practitioner.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The reason I ask this is, more often than not, in the situations of a potential child abuse case, the relevant stakeholders more often than not, tend to assume that the parent without the custody care and control should not be first informed, or any of the relevant information may not be revealed to him at the earliest instance, and there are situations or there are cases where in the event of parental alienation and child abuse cases, the parent that was affected by parental alienations will only know of the situations, being the last person in the situation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I can assure the Member that when a case involving a child enters the child protection case management agencies' ambit of work, they will put in their best efforts to engage both the child's biological parents for safety planning, where feasible – and I mentioned it earlier in response to Member Diana Pang's question, you may need one or the other parent to step in to part of the safety plan – especially if the parent is required to observe safeguards put in place, or is in a position to support the child's safety and well-being.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For cases that are taken up by the Protective Service in MSF, it will contact and engage both parents and/or all caregivers to ensure the child's safety and well-being, regardless of their marital status.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Cassandra Lee, did you raise your hand earlier?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: No, I am giving priority to those who have filed questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, Mr Andre Low, I know you filed a question for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My first question is actually relating the substance of my Parliamentary Question, which is filed for tomorrow, which has not been addressed – which is, I understand, Minister has mentioned many prospective actions that will be taken in response to the Review Panel's recommendations.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My question was more has there been any retrospective review of ongoing or past cases, whether it be in 2020 or recently, in response to the Review Panel's findings to make sure that we have not overlooked any other similar cases to avoid another tragedy?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think was implicit in Minister's response, but I would like to confirm if the officers continue to specialise in their respective specialties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think the first question it was in my main reply as well as in my supplementary question reply to Member Jackson Lam in terms of looking back and reaching out to organisations to surface cases that may be of concern.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But it is a service as a whole and there is a benefit in common protocols even as we seek to specialise in certain areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And the third is about strengthening the social work profession as a whole.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For protective work, as I said earlier, there is a real risk of burnout so lots of measures need to put in place, including care for the officers, time away from the frontlines, mental health support and constant training and refreshment so that we upskill and continue to be encouraged to continue this challenging work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we want to work with SUSS and our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to continue to train caring Singaporeans who want to come into this work of protecting vulnerable people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But as a whole, for the whole social sector, there continues to be a need for more social work professionals, social workers, caseworkers, counsellors and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And the work of the National Council of Social Service and the Ministry continues on this front to ensure that we have a steady pipeline.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And the reason I ask is because: the actual case load is to manage the child, but because of the coordination work that is required, because of the mind space that officer will need to have, I believe that the number of cases is still too high at 35.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have brought in auxiliary support services – not just increasing manpower, but brought in additional services to help transform and improve the way in which our Protective Service officers work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And I have said earlier that we will continue to expand.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have gone past Question Time by almost 20 minutes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I believe I have cleared all those Members who have filed PQs on this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will now just allow for two last supplementary questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, you have been raising your hand from day one, so you have the floor.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And I want to thank Minister Desmond Lee and Minister of State Goh Pei Ming for their heartfelt responses.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And I just wanted to ask my supplementary question as one of balance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my own personal dealings with the Social Service Officers (SSOs) and MSF, they are excellently diligent and hardworking people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They worked with me at 2.00 am on cases; likewise, Home Affairs officers visiting homes where there is abuse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I am genuinely concerned, and this is I am mounting my supplementary question that we do not forget the excellent hard work of the many diligent officers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And yes, there have been a number of difficult gaps that have aligned, and Megan is no longer with us, but I hope we will not throw the baby out with the bath water.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do not wish to underestimate the impact of Megan on all of us, but how do we walk this tight rope of encouraging and uplifting the morale of these excellent officers in both Ministries, while at the same time plugging the loopholes?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And the best way to support them is to affirm their work, know that while there were lapses and mistakes, we will continue to close the gap, learn from them and resolve collectively as a sector to do better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And that collective responsibility that Member Xie Yao Quan spoke about is important, even as we retain trust of members of the public through transparency and accountability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Other forms of support involve making sure that their well-being is taken care of, giving them respite, support, taking care of their mental well-being, training them well and effectively, putting in place standard operating procedures and protocols, both within the organisation and externally; supervision, support and mentorship so that they continue to do their work well.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: The responsibility is heavy and at the same time every police officer signs on knowing that it is a mission that he has to do for his fellow citizens and deliver that duty to the people who respect the uniform and respect the Police force for what they do.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: So, I thank the Member very much for the compliments for the professionalism and the commitment of all our police officers out there.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: I know every police officer will strive to do his best.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: Every case is important, and they have sworn to protect lives and to keep the nation, Singapore and Singaporeans, safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: At the same time, I think what the organisation and what I guess Members of Parliament can also help to do, is to acknowledge the hard work that they do.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: All Members of Parliament also have close relationship with police officers in your own constituencies.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: And I think that relationship, the close communication, understanding what are the challenges, the progress of work and perhaps, supporting if there is a need for them at the ground is important.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: From the Ministry, we will continue to support and make sure that feedback loops are closed.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: We will make sure that we hear and listen to the Police officers.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: And through the appraisal reports, for example, we do get feedback and how we can best support our officers.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: The second is, overall manpower allocation, we are also looking into how we can best allocate and optimise manpower assignments in terms of what are the areas of priority, areas of emphasis and to make the corresponding allocations or to grow the force where we need to.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I know you also filed a PQ for a subsequent Sitting.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You will be the final Member to ask a supplementary question on this.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also like to declare that I am the Executive Director of Campus Impact.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a social service agency that works with children, some of whom are child protection cases.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I acknowledge and I thank the Minister for sharing about the heavy emotional burden borne by child protection officers and welcome the news of a new social services coordination centre supported by technology to detect, sense make and connect the dots for cases from different touchpoints.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there specific indicators such as faster case detection, earlier intervention or reduce recurrence of child harm that will be tracked?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And how will MSF ensure that frontline social workers and community partners benefit directly from the improved coordination rather than being burdened by additional administrative layers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The social service coordination centre and the use of technology – these should augment the work of the child protection network, but in and of itself will not be a silver bullet.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We hope that with some technology, with coordination we can better focus on at-risk cases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because the workload is high, we encourage people to report and officers will be under strain to deal with many more cases that are surfaced, some of which would be false positives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And that is the way it is designed so that we take a look and dive a bit deeper.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But being able to connect some of these dots across multiple agencies and organisations will enable the system as a whole to be able to sense make better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sometimes, in its discrete self, a piece of information may not cause a flag to go up, but when you are able to better connect the dots, you might feel that, well, this is one which crosses the threshold; better go in and take a look.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As we consult with the sector, as we engage with them, as we work with them, we will better be able to unpack what capabilities we specifically seek to achieve.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: I may have misspoken, citing that the year this was introduced was 2020.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: [Pursuant to Standing Order No 22(3), provided that Members had not asked for questions standing in their names to be postponed to a later Sitting day or withdrawn, written answers to questions not reached by the end of Question Time are reproduced in the Appendix.]
